pages.title: Mandi Tool Belt rule book
pages.text:
Mandi Tool Belt: how to read the sample price board
The Mandi Tool Belt is a teaching project from the AI Engineering course by Ravi Shanker Singh (TechWithRavi). Everything on these three pages is invented for the course. The prices, charges and rules are not the rates or rules of any real market or market committee.
What the price board shows
The board lists one price a day for five vegetables: onion, tomato, potato, cabbage and brinjal. It covers three cities, Nashik, Pune and Indore, over ten sample days. Day 1 is the first sample day. The days are not calendar dates.
Each price is the modal price in rupees per kilogram. The modal price is the price at which most of that day's trade happened, so a few lots always sell above or below it.
Arrivals tell you how much of a vegetable reached the market that day. They are counted in quintals, and one quintal is 100 kilograms.
Questions the agent answers
The agent answers price questions from the board, explains the charges a buyer pays on top of the price, and converts between bags, crates and kilograms. The charges are on the Buyer charges page. Bag and crate sizes are on the Bags, crates and quintals page.
Rounding
Every bill is worked out to the paisa. It is rounded to the nearest rupee only at the very end, when the buyer pays.

pages.title: Buyer charges - Mandi Tool Belt
pages.text:
Buyer charges
Invented for the AI Engineering course. These are not the charges of any real market.
Commission
A buyer pays the commission agent 4 percent of the goods value. The goods value is the quantity in kilograms multiplied by the price per kilogram.
A bulk buyer pays 3 percent instead of 4 percent when one bill is for more than 10 quintals of the same vegetable.
Market fee
Every bill also carries a market fee of 1 percent of the goods value. The fee pays for the yard, the lights and the weighbridge.
Loading charge
Loading costs Rs 12 for each bag or crate that porters carry to the buyer's vehicle. Loose loads cost Rs 25 per quintal to load.
How a bill adds up
Total bill = goods value + commission + market fee + loading charge.
Example: 2 bags of potatoes weigh 100 kg. At Rs 20 per kg the goods value is Rs 2,000. The commission is Rs 80, the market fee is Rs 20 and loading is Rs 24, so the total bill is Rs 2,124.

pages.title: Bags, crates and quintals - Mandi Tool Belt
pages.text:
Bags, crates and quintals
Invented for the AI Engineering course. Real markets use many different bag sizes.
How much one bag or crate holds
Onion: one bag holds 50 kg.
Potato: one bag holds 50 kg.
Tomato: one crate holds 25 kg.
Cabbage: one sack holds 40 kg.
Brinjal: one crate holds 20 kg.
The quintal
Arrivals and bulk orders are counted in quintals. One quintal is 100 kg, so one quintal of onions is two bags. To turn quintals into kilograms, multiply by 100.
Grades
The price board shows grade A, the main quality of the day. Grade B lots are smaller or slightly damaged and usually sell for less. The board does not list grade B prices.
